https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-earthquak.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IjKD About 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for Image: Luisa Gonzalez/REUTERS Advertisement Rescuers worked through a third straight night with time ticking towards the 72-hour mark since a powerful earthquake hit Colombia. That's the period aid agencies consider most critical for finding survivors alive, though it can stretch longer if trapped people have access to food and water. "We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse. He said crews were still detecting signs of life beneath the rubble and urged speed: "Every minute is vital." Rescue workers ask for silence as they search for survivors at the site of collapsed buildings Image: Raul Arboleda/AFP The latest on the Colombia earthquake The death toll from the quake has climbed to 265, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday. De la Espriella said roughly 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for, though a crowdsourced tracking site used by families put the number of missing far higher, at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected in total, he said. The magnitude 7.4 quake — the strongest to hit Colombia in decades — struck on Monday morning near San Jose del Palmar in the northwestern Choco region. It tore through cities across western Colombia, with Cali and Pereira among the hardest hit, along with Manizales and Quibdo. In Cali, volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez described teams pausing every 30 minutes to listen for survivors. "So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead," she told AFP. Officials say 140 buildings collapsed entirely and thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed. Families grapple with human toll In Palmira, Santiago Lloreda told Reuters the quake killed his mother and his 13-month-old daughter, Salma, who was too young to have fingerprints on file and would need to be identified through DNA testing. He described his mother as the family's caretaker, saying she "gave everything up to look after the baby." A man who only gave the news agency his first name, Ricardo, traveled from Miami to recover his sister's body and said his niece was awaiting surgery for a fractured skull, jaw and leg, and a collapsed lung: "She's alive. We know she's going to get better." Colombia races against time after worst quake in a decade To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Thousands have been left homeless, with many sleeping outdoors in parks or emergency shelters set up in schools and sports arenas, either because their homes were destroyed or out of fear of aftershocks. Colombia's geological service has recorded 130 aftershocks since Monday's quake. International aid set to pour in Response efforts have been especially difficult in Choco, the quake's epicenter, a remote and impoverished region already strained by decades of conflict and displacement. Additionally, lost cell service has made it hard to assess damage in communities reachable only by river. "This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council. And UN resident coordinator María Jose Torres said in a statement Tuesday that aid groups already working in the region on an earlier peace effort were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief. The United States has pledged more than $15 million and sent response teams. Mexico has sent military aircraft carrying nearly 20 tons of food along with security personnel, with more aid and rescue specialists on standby. El Salvador's president offered two planes carrying 100 tons of supplies, and a search-and-rescue team from Mexico said it arrived directly from Venezuela, which faced its own major earthquakes in June . Quake response provides test for new Colombian president De la Espriella, inaugurated just three days before the earthquake struck, declared an economic emergency and three days of national mourning, and pledged to establish a fund to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure. "This is undoubtedly a tragedy of immense proportions," he said. "Our efforts are focused on those who remain missing." He has not yet detailed what the economic emergency measures will involve. Notably, de la Espriella won office on a platform of reduced public spending and a tougher security approach. Analyst Tiziano Breda, of the conflict-monitoring group ACLED, told Reuters that de la Espriella had campaigned in part on cutting funding to the country's disaster-response agency — the same unit now leading the emergency effort. Experts have cautioned that more seismic activity is possible, if not imminent. "Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," Rodrigo Leon Loya, a seismologist at the University of the Andes, told AP. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources," he warned. Edited by: Rob Turner Don't let the algorithm hide the news. Photograph: Adam Hunger/AP NHL NHL star Alex Ovechkin appears in campaign ad for pro-Putin United Russia party Capitals star is long-time supporter of Russian leader Ovechkin is NHL’s all-time leading goalscorer Robert Mackey and Tom Lutz Mon 14 Sep 2026 23.53 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Alex Ovechkin, the NHL’s all-time leading goalscorer , has appeared in a campaign ad for the United Russia party, which supports Vladimir Putin, as he prepares for the new hockey season. The Russian business newspaper Vedomosti published images of the Washington Capitals star alongside pro-Putin figures such as Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, the leading parliamentary candidate on United Russia’s list, and Margarita Simonyan, the editor-in-chief of the propaganda network RT. Alex Ovechkin is now the NHL’s greatest goalscorer. It’s debatable what else he is Read more Ovechkin is a longtime supporter of Putin. In 2017, he launched Putin Team , a social movement that he hoped would unite “people who are proud of their country and want to make Russia stronger”. He also praised the Russian leader’s “trust in and respect for his people, his fairness [and] righteousness, and the fact that he really cares”. The 40-year-old was more cautious about his backing of Putin after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He said he hoped the war “was going to be over and we are going to be living in a good world”, although he still said that Putin was “my president”. Hundreds of thousands of people have been killed in the war that followed the invasion. Ovechkin signed a one-year contract extension with the Capitals in July. The Capitals selected him with the first overall pick in the 2004 NHL draft and he has played his entire NHL career with them, winning the Stanley Cup as the team’s captain in 2018. In 2025, he scored his 895th goal , passing Wayne Gretzky’s all-time scoring record, a mark that had stood since 1999 and one few believed would ever be broken. Photograph: Salahuddin/Reuters View image in fullscreen Khan’s sisters Aleema Khanum, Uzma Khanum and Noreen Niazi among supporters of the former Pakistan PM in Rawalpindi last December. Photograph: Salahuddin/Reuters Pakistan Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi Mon 21 Sep 2026 10.48 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release. The lawyer for the three sisters, Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order. Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khan was arrested and held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release. His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment for an eye condition . The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government. None of Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison. Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father Read more Aleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore. According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken. By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar. He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things. “We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.” While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir , who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which was widely documented as rigged , allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power. Speaking to the Guardian last week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison. Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”. Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician and there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amid an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread. Prisoner number 804: the plot to erase Imran Khan Read more Khan’s party has faced constant harassment over the past three years , with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics. Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. Over the weekend, the capital of Pakistan , Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city. “Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.” Explore more on these topics Pakistan Imran Khan South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen New Zealand’s prime minister and National party leader Christopher Luxon speaks at the election night function at the Viaduct events centre in Auckland on Saturday. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP New Zealand election 2026 New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with election ‘too close to call’ National party will be largest in parliament but ultimate shape of next government won’t be settled for some time Eva Corlett in Auckland Sat 7 Nov 2026 20.00 EST First published on Sat 7 Nov 2026 08.48 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc. On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon , managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties. But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November. Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them. With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind. Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin. National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote. Labour, led by Chris Hipkins , secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government. View image in fullscreen Labour leader, Chris Hipkins, speaks to supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt on Saturday. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”. “As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour. The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high ⁠inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time. Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition. Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties. The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”. “It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.” New Zealand heads for election cliffhanger with minor party cast as kingmaker Read more In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote. However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang. National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance. That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs. On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats. With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition. The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime. “For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.” Explore more on these topics New Zealand election 2026 New Zealand Asia Pacific New Zealand politics Christopher Luxon Chris Hipkins Māori news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story New Zealand election coalition talks will likely take weeks – as it happened Gangs, gaffes and two guys named Chris: why I’m glued to the 2026 New Zealand election contest New Zealand heads for election cliffhanger with minor party cast as kingmaker In New Zealand’s bellwether seat, what are locals thinking as a knife-edge poll looms? https://hvg.hu/kkv/20261110_rogan-antal-.text: Hét, összesen 142 millió forint értékű megrendelésnél gondolja úgy a Minisztérium, hogy jogtalan lehetett a közbeszerzés mellőzése, vagy a szerződés tárgyának kiterjesztése. Közbeszerzési jogorvoslati eljárásokat kezdeményezett a Nemzeti Kommunikációs Hivatal (NKOH) a Miniszterelnökség 2023-2026 közötti tanácsadói megrendelései miatt – közölte a hivatal az MTI-vel. Összesen 142 millió forint értékű megrendelésről van szó. A hivatal azt jelezte: a rendelkezésre álló dokumentumok alapján felmerült a gyanú, hogy a Miniszterelnökség számos alkalommal olyan szolgáltatásokat rendelt meg a p2m Informatika Szolgáltató Kft. és a p2m Consulting Szolgáltató és Tanácsadó Kft. alkotta konzorciumtól, amelyek nem tartoztak a szervezetfejlesztési célú keretmegállapodás tárgyi hatálya alá. A p2m-ről korábban többször írt a HVG is. Amikor a Nemzeti Kommunikációs Hivatalt még Rogán Antal vezette, előbb arról cikkeztünk, hogy 265 szervezetfejlesztési munkából mind a 265 ugyanahhoz a cégcsoporthoz került , majd miután ezt megírtuk, további három hónappal később már 281-ből 281-nél tartottak . A p2m-cégek 2021 második negyedévétől 2025 harmadik negyedévéig több mint nettó 18 milliárd forintnyi megbízást kaptak az opciós kereteket is beleszámolva. A 2024-es költségszerkezet alapján azt a következtetést vontuk le, hogy a cégek elsősorban nem termelőként, hanem közvetítőként működtek: az állami megbízásokból befolyó milliárdok nagy része továbbáramlott más vállalkozásokhoz, miközben a haszon a tulajdonosoknál koncentráltan jelent meg. A cég annak a Szabad Tamásnak az érdekeltségébe tartozott, aki 2004-ben alapítója lett a Lounge Consultingnak, ahonnan 2012-ben szállt ki, amikor már egykori osztálytársa, Balásy Gyula is szerepet vállalt benne, és később is több üzleti összefonódás volt kettejük cégei között. A hivatal azt írta az MTI-nek, hogy a hét megrendelés, amelyre most jogorvoslatot kezdeményeztek, többek között munkaerőpiaci és migrációs kutatásokra, a digitális játékipar lehetőségeinek elemzésére, az Otthon Start Program stratégiai felülvizsgálatára, valamint külső szervezetek átvilágítására irányult. Az NKOH álláspontja szerint ezek a feladatok érdemben eltértek az eredetileg versenyeztetett szervezetfejlesztési szolgáltatásoktól, ezért felmerül a közbeszerzési eljárás jogtalan mellőzésének, illetve a szerződés tárgya jogellenes kiterjesztésének lehetősége. Az NKOH közölte azt is, hogy vizsgálatuk nem korlátozódik a most kifogásolt hét megrendelésre. A hivatal meglátása szerint az elmúlt években a Miniszterelnökség a p2m-cégektől további olyan tanulmányokat is megrendelt, amelyek esetében szintén felmerül a közbeszerzési szabályok megsértése. Tanács Zoltán tudományos és technológiai miniszter még október 21-én azt közöte, hogy a p2m Consulting Kft. szerződései kapcsán nyomozást rendeltek el, miután a minisztérium feljelentést tett. A p2m-cégek ügyeiben a Miniszterelnökség még egy feljelentést tett szeptemberben : a feljelentés tárgya ott is hasonló volt a mostanihoz, a kancellária megítélése szerint a 17 egyedi megrendelésből 16 nem tartozott a szervezetfejlesztési keretszerződések tárgykörébe. Ennek a 16 szerződésnek az együttes összege bruttó 455 millió forintra rúg.

Read below for a roundup of headlines and analysis from Germany on Tuesday, November 10, 2026: Skip next section Merz, Magyar look to revive German-Hungarian ties 11/10/2026 November 10, 2026 Merz, Magyar look to revive German-Hungarian ties The two leaders discussed strengthening German-Hungarian relations Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar pledged to strengthen relations between their countries during talks in Berlin, announcing plans for closer cooperation on energy, defense and trade. Merz described the meeting, attended by several ministers from both governments, as part of a fresh start in relations between Germany and Hungary. "The German and Hungarian histories are closely intertwined," Merz said, adding that he wanted to use the momentum of Hungary's new government to revive bilateral ties. Magyar highlighted the significance of his visit taking place around November 9 —the anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. "It is a very important day in the life of the German people," Magyar said, adding that Hungary was proud of the role it had played in those historic events . In August 1989, hundreds of East Germans escaped to Austria during the Pan-European Picnic on the Hungarian border. Hungary subsequently opened its border to East German refugees in September, allowing tens of thousands to flee to the West and helping accelerate the collapse of communist rule in East Germany. Around 600 escaped through a temporarily opened border gate, helping pave the way for the fall of the Iron Curtain (FILE: 19/08/1989) Image: Votava/dpa/picture alliance Turning to economic relations, Merz said Germany was Hungary's largest trading partner and welcomed what he called positive signals from Budapest about improving conditions for German companies. Merz also offered to help Hungary reduce its dependence on Russian energy imports by providing access to capacity at German liquefied natural gas terminals and sharing expertise in renewable energy. "The stars are very favorable," Magyar said, referring to prospects for strengthening the countries' already close economic and cultural ties. Magyar welcomed the offer but stressed that prices would be crucial. Edited by: Zac Crellin https://p.dw.com/p/5PIy8 Skip next section Aigner on course for presidency as AfD criticizes snub 11/10/2026 November 10, 2026 Aigner on course for presidency as AfD criticizes snub Richard Connor Ilse Aigner is highly likely to become Germany's first female president after securing support from the governing conservatives and Social Democrats (SPD) , alongside a recommendation from the Green Party leadership. The governing parties already hold an estimated majority of around 50 votes in the Federal Convention, which elects the president. Green backing would substantially widen that margin, making a first-round victory on January 30 highly likely. Aigner, Bavaria 's state parliament president from the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) , received standing ovations from lawmakers of her party and its sister party, the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) . The SPD, which has formally endorsed her, also welcomed her with applause. But Aigner's decision to decline an invitation from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) prompted criticism from co-leader Alice Weidel . "Apparently, we cannot expect political impartiality from Ilse Aigner," Weidel said. Aigner's team cited AfD lawmaker Beatrix von Storch's disparaging response to her nomination as the reason for declining. Aigner herself did not address the dispute during her press statement. The Federal Convention comprises Bundestag lawmakers and an equal number of delegates chosen by state parliaments. It will elect a successor to President Frank-Walter Steinmeier . Ilse Aigner could become Germany's first female president To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Edited by: Zac Crellin https://p.dw.com/p/5PIk3 Skip next section Aigner says she could be 'something of a first' as president 11/10/2026 November 10, 2026 Aigner says she could be 'something of a first' as president Richard Connor Backed by the CDU/CSU and SPD, Aigner could become Germany's first female president Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance Germany's conservative presidential candidate Ilse Aigner has highlighted various ways she would break new ground if elected as the country's first female president. Aigner was nominated to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in the January 30 election. She presented herself to parliamentary groups and highlighted her route into politics through an apprenticeship and technical work rather than university as one difference from predecessors. Aigner would also be the first president from Bavaria's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU). "In many ways, I am something of a first — or could be," the Bavarian state parliament president said. "And I'm also single — I always mention that too." Defending democracy would be her central priority, she said during an appearance with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and CSU leader Markus Söder. "I want to stand up for democracy — for me, that really is a mission," Aigner said, warning that democracy was under pressure "from within and from outside." She pledged to build bridges, overcome divisions and remain close to ordinary people. "I will be one of them," she said. Edited by: Zac Crellin https://p.dw.com/p/5PIis Skip next section Aigner to meet with CDU/CSU, Greens and SPD in Bundestag Published 11/10/2026 Published November 10, 2026 last updated 11/10/2026 last updated November 10, 2026 Aigner to meet with CDU/CSU, Greens and SPD in Bundestag The top candidate to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president, Ilse Aigner , is set to visit the Bundestag, where she will meet with the center-right CDU/CSU bloc, the Social Democrats and the Greens. She has said she will not meet with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) after one of their top members called her nomination a "disgrace." She also has not received an official invitation from the Left party. Aigner was officially nominated by the CDU/CSU bloc , also known as the Union, on Monday, practically securing her future as German president. She already has support from the SPD and Greens. The official vote will take place on January 30. The president is chosen by the Bundestag. Despite being the highest political office in the country, it is a largely ceremonial role.
